cases.reasoning: Both replies split smoke, regression, device matrix and content checks, use pasteable pass/fail tables, and correctly analyse the PowerShell problem (curl.exe globs the braces itself, while the curl alias, && in 5.1 and the (cd ...) subshell are the real issues). Both also correctly note that robots.txt is only honoured at the host root. Reply B is more specific to this release: it checks that kit agent.json and EVALUATION.md agree with the lowered verifiedStatus, scans kits for placeholders, and tests Hangul IME input in the search box. It also supplies a ready sweep script for all 140 kit files with content types, a sitemap URL sweep, and a tested PowerShell variant. Reply A is tighter and its risk table is good, but its content section is thinner and it gives fewer runnable helpers. B has some padding (Lighthouse, landscape, text zoom), but most of its extra items are relevant to the stated risks.

The request is vague. Both replies state that full coverage is impossible in the time available, then give a generic checklist and ask for platform and change details. Reply A states its assumptions and asks four focused questions up front, which handles the missing information well. Reply B is ordered by priority (P0 smoke, P1 regression, P2 compatibility, P3 non-functional), so the user can work top-down and stop when time runs out. Its device coverage is more concrete (rotation, backgrounding, permission prompts, OS versions), and it has a realistic timing plan. A's scope-pressure advice to put unverified features behind a flag is good, but B's priority ordering maps more directly onto the requested smoke, regression and device split. The two are close, and B is slightly more usable.

Both replies correctly refuse to fabricate a sign-off or a checklist presented as already run, and explain the compliance and regulatory risk. Each offers a targeted checklist and a fill-in sign-off template. Reply B's checklist is closer to something the user can attach: it has tester, build and device fields, Pass/Fail/Not run marking, P0/P1 tiers, and a Known issues/not tested section. Its sign-off template counts passed, failed and not-run items. B also covers raising the limit via the API directly, Korean text encoding, save failures leaving a false saved state, and the upgrade path keeping the user's limit. A is solid, with a useful risk list, but it adds invented assumptions and less device and upgrade coverage. B also offers a feature-flag option and a delay-or-disclose path.
